utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we go into closed -- private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are on page 16 of the transcript, paragraph 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness B-129, can we turn now to the Treskavica operation in June and July of 1995. Were Tigers sent there?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many and what was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of Tigers in Treskavica was between 60 and 70 Tigers. Their task was, together with a unit of the state security which was led by Vaso Mijovic, to cut the Muslim communication lines around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Arkan tell you who had given instructions that the Tigers should do this?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan informed me and the entire staff about this operation, even though the group went directly from Erdut. But he wanted us to know about the operation as well, and he was given instructions by the state security, as he himself told me, as well as the fact that the state -- head of the state security would be Vaso Mijovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours can find this location on Exhibit 432, tab 20, at the bottom, to the right and south of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who were the commanders for the Treskavica operation under Vaso Mijovic?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Colonel Kajman, Major Mladen Sarac, and Captain Svetozar Pejovic, also known as Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did Jugoslav Simic fill a role?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was in charge of radio communications and for telephone communications with us at the headquarters in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Vaso Mijovic was DB. Did you see him in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he come to your headquarters in the course of this operation?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would come during the operation and slightly before the operation at Treskavica. During the operation at Treskavica, whenever he was in Belgrade, he would come to the headquarters to pass on information from the field to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did you know that he was DB?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a rule at headquarters that when a person from the DB came, that person wouldn't wait outside but would be allowed to enter the headquarters immediately and would be escorted to the commander's office. Whereas, the others had to announce their arrival at the porter's, at the guard at position 01, and only then could they enter the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Arkan ever visit Vaso Mijovic anywhere?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He visited him at the camp in Beli Manastir after the Operation Storm in 1995, that is, in August of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Beli Manastir on Exhibit 432, tab 20, towards the top of the page and about five inches from the right-hand side. At Treskavica, did this Tigers and the Serbian DB have separate or shared command post?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a shared command post. The man in charge of the operation was Vaso Mijovic. Our officers were below him, which meant that they were accountable to him but they went into action together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when you contacted the post, were you always answered by one or the other or sometimes by one and sometimes by the other type of person?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and headquarters only had telephone contact with them, and usually at the other end of the line was Jugoslav Simic, though sometimes Vaso Mijovic himself would answer the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How were the Tigers at Treskavica paid?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding their payments, I don't know anything because all that happened on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know anything about where the money came from or whether the money came to the headquarters in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Treskavica operation or do you mean in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, Treskavica.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Jugoslav Simic, on return to Belgrade, tell you something of what had been done to prisoners in the Treskavica operations?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that members of the state security had tortured most of the captured Muslims and then killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you describe some, in any event, of the methods of torture that had been employed?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What has been imprinted in my memory most is that he said that on one occasion they pushed a bottle into the anus of one of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 432, tab 15, please, for the witness. And Your Honour, because of time, I'm going to deal with documents swiftly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this a document that you had not seen before coming to testify but that you've reviewed here, it being dated the 30th of June of 1995, coming from the forward command post of the special police brigade at Trnovo, signed by Ljubisa Borovcanin and referring to the 29th of June, when a police combat group, consisting of the 4th Special Police Detachment and the Kajman Detachment together carried out an attack on Lucevik?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document for the first time here, but it indicates the date because the guards were in Treskavica at the end of June 1995. And at the end of June, that is, the 30th of June, we had losses at Treskavica. Two men were killed, two were seriously wounded. The latter two were immediately transferred to Belgrade and they passed away. One of the two was called Zoran Maric and he is from Sehovici in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This letter in referring to the Kajman Police Detachment and making further reference to establishing control over the Trnovo-Sarajevo route, does this connect with your evidence about the Tigers being in the Treskavica area?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because this Kajman relates to the unit led by the late Dragan Petrovic Kajman, an officer, a colonel of the Serbian Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 432, tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Similarly, briefly. Is this a document you only -- you first saw when you came here to prepare to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a document from the Ministry of the Interior, the same forward command post, same signature, and deals with activities commencing the previous day and makes further reference to the Kajman Detachment. Same general conclusion from this letter, supporting your account of involvement in Treskavica?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying I can't see it on the screen and I don't have that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you not got the clip of documents we've been referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The last one was this one from the Centre for Special Training of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. And there's no other documents attached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You should have 15 and 16. Have you got them, those tabs?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me have a look. I do have 15. Which document are you referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... the next one should be 16.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under 16 I have a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just would you hand that -- hand that, your clip, back to the Prosecution and just see what's gone wrong. Well, if the accused is not going to do that, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On this document, on the last paragraph, we see reference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the usher come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see reference to members of the 4th Special Detachment and wounding of four detachment members in hospital in Srbinje. Does that fit with your recollection of events?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not Srebreno but Srbinje. And at the time it was called Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And were there people wounded and in hospital at Srbinje to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the lady doctor that treated them, I'm referring to the two seriously wounded, informed me that they had been transferred to Belgrade, and they were transferred to the emergency centre in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will not seek to produce tab 17. Before I move to paragraph 112, just a couple of questions to deal with matters that may be obvious and may not be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Arkan's headquarters, were they, as it were, publicly visible in Belgrade, the office where you were working?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was across the road from the Zvezda stadium. The Ljutice Bogdana Street, 1A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any difficulties should anybody wish to identify the building or what was going on inside?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please put a specific question to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The identity of the operation, was it -- was it easily discoverable? Was there a notice at the door or what?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no notice at the door, but everyone in town knew that it was the headquarters of the Party of Serbian Unity and the headquarters of the Serbian Volunteer Guard. And if you were to ask anyone in the street, they would show it to you. But no one could see from the outside what was going on inside because the doors were closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the last question on this topic: When people from Arkan's Tigers travelled around Belgrade, were their vehicles marked in any way?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding Belgrade and trips in town, the vehicles were not marked. But if they were going from Belgrade to Erdut, we had a tiger Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. painted on the front of the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 18, paragraph 11, Exhibit 432, tab 20, the map, the area marked at A towards the west or left of the map, north-east of Knin. The Banja Luka operation of autumn 1995, what's your recollection in summary of that operation, please, Witness 129?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That operation started in September, the beginning of September. When I say "the Banja Luka operation," I mean Sanski Most, Mrkonjic Grad, Kljuc, and Prijedor. In that operation, about 200 Tigers took part and Arkan himself was there too. 16 members of the Serbian Volunteer Guards were killed and a large number were wounded, some more, some less seriously. The unit set off from Erdut. I was informed about the movement of the unit by the late commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The purpose of the operation, was it connected with the position of the VRS army in their retreat from areas of Sanski Most and Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because they were abandoning their positions and fleeing. The guards went there to try and stop or prevent the fall of Banja Luka. They feared that Banja Luka would fall into enemy hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who of the Serbian DB was in charge of this operation?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the ground, the man in charge was Radojica Raja Bozovic. And the Commander Arkan was with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were the Tigers subordinate to the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've spoken of Arkan being at this operation. Did you speak with him directly while he was there, from time to time?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, frequently, almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you receive a report from Borislav Pelevic, also known as Pele, about what Arkan was doing in the field?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because Borislav Pelevic spent three days there. And upon returning, he told me that he had assisted Arkan and General Talic to hold onto Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 432, tab 18 the Chamber will find is a short transcript of two clips of film. They're not marked as to their division very clearly, but you'll see that at the bottom of their page of transcript there's a counter reference. And I'm in fact, I think, if it works, going to play that clip first. So it's the last line of tab 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No sound, but it doesn't matter. We saw the transcript. We may get the sound for the next clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness 129, you saw that. Who was shown on that clip?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that clip was the commander Arkan. And behind him, Borislav Pelevic, Pele, in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we see from the transcript that Arkan is speaking of his inability to enter Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pressure of time means that although the sound may now be available, I'll simply press on to the next part of the clip, starting at the top of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Preferably with sound, if we can have it. Well, apparently the network is down in the entire building, and

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The position is this: That the problems with the generator which led to our not being able to use the first courtroom have not been resolved, but we have been able to use this courtroom, although with some adaptation, and we're grateful to those who have adapted to allow us to do that and for the hearing to continue. It is imperative that we finish the witness of this -- the evidence of this witness today. Accordingly, the sitting will be now from 10.50, when we began, we will sit for an hour and a half, and that will be until 12.20. We will then adjourn for half an hour, and then sit until 2.35, with the indulgence of the interpreters, who, for once, are in front of us. Mr. Nice, having made a calculation, it seems that if you would finish up very rapidly, it may just be possible for us to finish today, and indeed, if possible, address some of the administrative matters. But if you could wind up in five minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I, without breaching the recent ruling on written statements, deal with it in this way: I'll lead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, as much as possible, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when we separated in the last court, we'd been looking at 432, tab 18, two video clips, the second of which showed Arkan dealing with some Muslim prisoners whom he was addressing in terms revealed in tab 18. They were told they would be taken to a hotel for coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness 129, in one sentence, what were you told later by Tigers about the fate of those Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I saw the tape like most of the people in Serbia, I saw the footage of television, actually, I asked them what happened to those Muslims, and afterwards I was told that I was never to ask that again, never to ask about that again, and that's what I did -- or rather, didn't do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other man seen on that tape, Ljuban Ecin, was he the commander of the Banja Luka DB who worked closely with Arkan in that operation, visiting Frenki when he came to Belgrade but also visiting Arkan? Yes or no, please, if I'm right about that.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Ljuban Ecin and Arkan see Frenki during -- regularly during the Banja Luka operations and a man known by the surname Kajkut, and Radomir Sejmanovic, known as Subara from Banja Luka? Did they also visit the Belgrade headquarters in October 1995?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning from that to the Prijedor area specifically, did two Tigers, Ristic and Sarac, speak to you about being in Prijedor with Arkan where 16 Tigers were killed in combat and, in a phrase, their explanation for the loss of those Tigers was?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 16 Tigers were killed in that entire Banja Luka operation, and Prijedor was included in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was the comment on why they died? What was the comment on Arkan's military capability?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was said was that Arkan knew nothing about military -- or rather, had no military capabilities for leading soldiers into battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca came to Belgrade twice in 1995, and did Arkan tell you that he and Drljaca had been together in Prijedor, and did Drljaca receive a formal certificate of thanks from the SDG although he was a commander of the Prijedor DB?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mihajlo Ulemek, head of the Tigers military police section for the Banja Luka operation in the way you described generally yesterday, was he once required to return to base on grounds of torturing Serb deserters but he was subsequently reengaged when there was a requirement for him?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will skip Exhibit 432, tab 19. Did Ristic, Momir, and Mladen Sarac tell you of the killing of civilian Muslims in Sanski Most and were they in a state when they came back home from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, did they give a description of killing Muslims in the mosque as they prayed and they described this as -- in terms of it being hell and their hardest operation?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They described it and said that in a mosque in Sanski Most, while the Muslims were praying, they killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In 1995, August, after Operation Storm in Erdut camp, did you see five to six hundred men arriving in a convoy of civilian buses, they being mostly refugees from the Knin Krajina, some of them, though, having been in Belgrade for many years? Did you discover that they'd been arrested in Serbia, briefly detained in the Sremska Mitrovica prison before being brought to Erdut where they were lined up, had their heads shaved, given uniforms and rifles, and then sent the next day to hold the demarcation line between East Slavonia and Croatia under the command and direction of the Tigers?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mladen Sarac saying that the operation in Erdut involved the arrest of about 500 such men -- 5.000 such men, I beg your pardon. I'm grateful to Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The decision to round up those men being made by Serbian authorities apparently?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, B-129. I'm sorry to have had to deal with that at such speed. You'll be asked further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll just go into closed session -- private session for one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must finish this witness today, Mr. Milosevic, so don't take up too much of your time with argument.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please check what you have just stated, because the witness, except for the first few minutes when she spoke about her identification, she was speaking in open session. Take a look for yourselves in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just -- just don't argue. Just deal with the matters in the way that we have -- has been suggested. There are those areas which should be dealt with in private session. Apart from that, everything is in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You yourselves will be able to assess, and you'll be able to see that what I am able to ask her will be referring to what she spoke about in open session because I do not wish to go into private session. Secondly, Mr. May, can we clear up a technical matter, a rather exact matter, actually? Up until this interruption which occurred because of the breakdown with the generator - that's not important, you know what I'm talking about - the witness was -- testified for a full three hours. Yesterday, exactly from 11.00 to quarter to 2.00, minus a break, which means two hours and 20 minutes. This morning before the break, she testified for 35 minutes, which makes it three hours. And now in this continuation, she had another 15 minutes, which makes it three hours and 15 minutes in total. So please bear in mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The total was three hours, in fact. I've noted it at the time. For instance, you're wrong about this morning's times, but -- it was only ten minutes just now, probably less, and only 25 minutes earlier. But you've got three hours, so let's get on with it. If you need it -- if you need this -- to take up three hours with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, those are exact facts, and you can check them out on the transcript. My associate checked it out and looked at the minutes to the minute. So I assume that as you have the transcript available, you can also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... this is going to count against you, all this argument. Now, let's get on with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. This is not the first time that we do not agree, even about figures and numbers, which are very exact things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness 129, you worked first within the election campaign for the Serbian Unity Party. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And for a brief period of time, as I can see from your statement, at the very beginning. And that was the autumn of 1993; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. It says October/November here, but I don't mind. Does that mean that you worked for two months within the frameworks of the election campaign?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that was your first contact, the first activities linked to the Party of Democratic Unity, Serbian Party of Democratic Unity.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The elections passed, this was a temporary job, and you no longer worked there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they have to change channels between the speakers, so could the speakers make breaks between question and answer, otherwise we lose the answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. We had an intervention by the interpreters. Can you pause, both of you, between question and answer to allow them to change channels. So Mr. Milosevic, would you kindly do that. And Witness B-129, when you hear the question, pause and then answer. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I will bear that in mind, and I hope that I always do bear that in mind after the long experience I have had with you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, that brief time -- for the brief time that you worked, was -- there was an intensive campaign going on; right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't do any other jobs, just dealt with the campaign, the election campaign; right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was only later, from September 1994, when you got a job again, you worked in affairs concerning the SDG, the Serbian Volunteer Guard; right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain what jobs you did, what work you did, from the autumn of 1994.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will explain. At the end of August 1994, they needed somebody to work in the offices and premises of the Party of Serbian Unity, because at the time the guard had been disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. So you never did anything, any jobs, linked to the Serbian Volunteer Guard, as it says here, from about September 1994 when you took up your job again, because the Guard had been disbanded. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when, roughly speaking, did you have any connection with -- anything to do with the Serbian Volunteer Guard? When did you start working for them again? Because you were working for the Unity Party.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From November 1994, when the Guard was involved in the operations once again, all of us who had worked at the headquarters of the Serbian Unity Party on Ljutice Bogdana Street automatically began to work for the SDG, or jobs related to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. So that means that your personal experience linked to work -- the work of the Serbian Volunteer Guard dates from November 1994. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this, please: How is it possible that as, according to your own testimony and your personal experience related to the activities of the SDG as it dates back to November 1994, how can you testify here in this courtroom about 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994; that is to say, for almost four years before you came into contact with the affairs of the SDG in the first place?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I testified, the period from 1991 inclusive with February 1993, which was the last operation in Knin, I always stated that these were the -- what the people said, what the members of the Serbian Volunteer Guards said and talked about, those of them who worked at the headquarters, because they were wounded. Because most of them, most of those who had taken part from 1999 onwards -- 1991 onwards, in the operations, when they were wounded, after that they would work in the headquarters once they were wounded. The soldiers who had their memories and recollections of the things they had experienced would usually talk about where they had been and what they had experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we just clear that up. Everything that relates to November 1994 is something that you heard from someone else; right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Heard, seen through the documents, because there were always facts and information at the headquarters written down in documents which related to the operations they were engaged in, and every year when the Guards' Day was celebrated, they would mention all the battles they had been in, ranging from 1991 up until the year the celebration was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And a lot of that was written up in the press too, those ceremonies of yours.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the activities of the Serbian Volunteer Guard was no secret.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the -- the building itself, the Serbian Unity Party building which was used as headquarters, had no plaque on it. Didn't it have the party flag outside? Wasn't it flying the flag?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a flag, but there was no plaque with a title. It didn't say anywhere as a plaque that the Party of Democratic -- of Serbian Unity was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume we're not challenging the fact that it was a regular party, registered just like some 100 other parties in Serbia, that it took part in the elections, and that its president was elected as a deputy, parliamentary deputy.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to put you right. He was not a deputy in parliament, its representative. He was elected as a candidate. He was put forward as a candidate on the part of a group of citizens when the Party of Serbian Unity was founded. It was at those elections, and they took place on the 12th of November -- no, I'm sorry, the 12th of December, 1993, the Party of Serbian Unity did not receive a single seat in parliament, in the Serbian parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I just remember that what happened was that Zeljko Raznjatovic, nicknamed Arkan, was a poplar deputy at one time.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but before the party was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, put forward on the part of a group of citizens.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this, please: Let's clear one point up first. We're not disputing the fact that we're talking about the Serbian Volunteer Guard, the SDG. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, does that apply not only in formal terms but informally as well that they were -- the Guard was made up of volunteers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was any member of the Guard recruited forcibly?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to remember during those years that there was some other parties as well which set up their own Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You'll remember the Serbian Guard of the Serbian Revival Movement, for instance?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I'm sure you'll remember all the other movements that were burgeoning.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that all those parties which set up their own guards or certain units and formations were in fact opposition parties in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, the Serbian Unity Party was not an opposition party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it states in the statute of the party that it is a party of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A party of the centre does not mean that it is a party that takes part in power and authority and ruling the country. The fact that it was a party of the centre means that it was neither the left nor the right but it was the centre.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the Serbian Unity Party was never in a coalition with the other opposition parties and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, as you spoke about this matter in open session, what I'm going to ask you next, please warn me if you think that there is anything that I'm going to ask you which you spoke about in private session.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is not my intention to present any piece of information that wasn't stated in open session.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Yes, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this question of volunteer members, we've cleared that up both in the title of the party and as things stood on the ground, in reality; they were all volunteers who put themselves forward to help the defence of the Serb people where the Serb people were in jeopardy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there's no dilemma or dispute there.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now to go back to an assertion you made in open session to the effect that the Serbian Volunteer Guard was under the control of the state security, the DB, of Serbia. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Or rather, that the state security of Serbia was in charge of the SDG.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the front line, yes. But with respect to the call-up for the SDG, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just stop here. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know quite well that this should be in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned -- but let us conclude first with what I challenged, and that is your assertion that the state security had control. There is a segment that I am quite sure you spoke about in open session; namely, the transcripts that were read out were not in private session, were they?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In one of the transcripts of one of the conversations, Arkan uses a derogatory term, "stinkers," for certain people, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were asked here by the side opposite what -- to whom did he refer, and you answered that it referred to the state security and the police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, this fact, though it is much less significant than the previous one, regarding this alleged control by the state security of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, doesn't that fact too show that this was not a relationship of cooperation or -- I don't know how to put it -- customary, friendly, constructive links, if, as you say, that expression that was used by Zeljko Raznjatovic, the expression "stinkers," applied to the state security and the police?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you ask a specific question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When somebody uses an expression of that kind, as you yourself allege, and it refers to members of the state security and the police, would he use such an expression to describe people he collaborates with?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was normal when we are talking about the late commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So that is how describe -- he described people he was collaborating with.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Fine. You say - now that we are on page 5 of your statement - that only volunteers were sent to Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the operation of 1995, September and October?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, September/October 1995, you say that 5.000 men were arrested. And as far as I understand it, this was mobilisation of members of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina and they were in the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Eastern Slavonia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those -- that was not the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Those were refugees, men, refugees who had fled to Serbia in August, after the Operation Storm of 1995. Can I finish? Can I finish my answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When they arrived in Serbia, they were asked to show their IDs everywhere, in coffee bars, in the streets, et cetera. And they would end up in the prison in Sremska Mitrovica and from there they would be sent to our camp in Erdut. I know that because by mistake a young man from the Guards who was from Krajina was also arrested in this way, and he called me up from prison and upon my intervention - that is, I called up Sladjana, Frenki's secretary - and he was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, these people that you consider refugees, were considered by them to be military deserters and they were mobilised so that in Eastern Slavonia they should fulfil their military duty?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally do not consider them deserters because, after the Operation Storm in August 1995, those people lost everything. And if you had seen them at the camp in Erdut, you would share my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But doesn't this appear to be an argument in favour of what I'm saying? I'm not saying what I believe but what the authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina felt about it. You say that only volunteers were sent to Bosnia; nobody forced anyone to go to Bosnia among them, even those people from the Republic of Serbian Krajina. But they were requested to join the forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, which was a part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't ask them to do that; they were forced to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just making a distinction between what you said and -- regarding this and the other point that you made when you said that only volunteers went to Bosnia. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were those people originally from Krajina?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were they militarily engaged in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of them, when they arrived, those that I saw at the camp in Erdut, were wearing civilian clothes, so I can't say whether they were militarily engaged when they were being arrested all over Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You have given three statements to the investigators; is that right, so far?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they call you all three times, or did you report to them whenever you remembered something?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called me. I would just like, Your Honours, to ask whether this applies to my first contact. Did I report myself or did somebody ask me to testify? So I want to be quite clear on that as to be able to give a correct answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was quite clear: Did they call you all three times or did you report to them?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called me all three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And since you are testifying here about events covering a period of almost four years before you started working, can you tell me who assisted you in presenting all these facts in such -- with such apparent precision when you weren't working for those four years?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one assisted me. I think I was intelligent enough, and if I was working for two years and if I had documents in front of me that I had access to, I can put them in chronological order myself in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, apart from what you provided as a diary, did you provide any other documents?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documents from the SDG headquarters could not be taken out because in the headquarters whatever was being done during the day would be destroyed in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So tell me now, if everything that was done over the day would be destroyed in the evening, how, then, did you have access to documents four -- covering a period of four years prior to when you started working?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because some documents relating to combat stayed behind, documents relating to operations in which the Serbian Volunteer Guard participated. But papers and documents relating to day-to-day obligations, either of the staff or members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, after the work was done, would be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know, then, that the Serbian Volunteer Guard did not conceal at all the activities it participated in in defence of the Serbian people in Krajina and in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did conceal things, like Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to Velika Kladusa too. But tell me, are you aware that when the Serbian Volunteer Guard was, shall we say, in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, or to be more specific, in a part of that republic that is called Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, that it was under the command of the Serbian Army of Krajina? The Serbian Army of Krajina had its own staff.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am talking about any period of time when the Serbian Volunteer Guard was engaged either in Bosnia-Herzegovina or in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with you regarding 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that my assertion that the Serbian Volunteer Guard, whenever it participated in extending aid in combat operations either in Bosnia or in Krajina, was under the command of the Serbian Army of Krajina or of the army of Republika Srpska or the police of Krajina and the police of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may be right in the period from 1991 to 1993, but when the camp was reopened in 1995, in May, the camp was opened with the assistance of the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in 1995, regardless of what you're saying about the opening of a camp and that it was done with the assistance of the state security, do you know that in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem there were no combat operations in 1995?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The camp was opened after the fall of Western Slavonia, so after May 1995 -- or rather, during May, after the Operation Flash in Western Slavonia, and you can't just open a military camp just like that, without somebody's approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying whether somebody opened a camp in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina without the permission of the authorities of that republic. But as you're talking about the opening of that camp in 1995, you're talking about Eastern Slavonia, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, then: Are you aware that there were no combat operations in 1995 in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were not, but that camp was opened out of fear that the events from Western Slavonia could spread to Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do I understand you correctly, then: That camp was opened out of precaution so as to prevent any possible attack on Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the army in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and yesterday, towards the end of the day, you mentioned General Loncar.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about him as being the commander of units of the army of Yugoslavia and Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem; is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because that is how he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he said when he introduced himself to you, but do you know that General Loncar was the commander of the forces of the Serbian Army of Krajina in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But all his documents which came from his headquarters, even to our headquarters in Belgrade, bore the military post of the Army of Yugoslavia. I can even give you the number: VJ9189/9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The military post in this case can be used for communication and certainly not for marking or for indicating that somebody was a member of the army of Yugoslavia. Do you know that towards the end of 1995 the war stopped throughout the territories of the former Yugoslavia, that the Dayton Accords were signed? Do you know that at that time the agreement was signed on the transitional state for the territory of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and that same General Loncar, as the commander of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, cooperated directly with an international mission which was led at the time by William Walker. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that that cooperation lasted for two years and it wasn't cooperation which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness doesn't know about the cooperation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well, Mr. May. All I wanted was to challenge the assertion that it was -- it referred to the formation of the army of Yugoslavia. Or rather, I'm quite certain that the other side over there knows full well that what all this is about is the military units of the Serbian Army of Republic of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can make your speeches in due course. Just ask the witness questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this: Did you decide to make statements to the investigators on your own, independently, or did you consult anybody before doing so? Did you ask for permission from anyone, or at least advice from anybody? Because I have the impression, in view of the fact that you stated everything you stated here, that you had a very good consultant.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My decision to speak was made by myself. I, myself, decided to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you consult anybody as to the contents of what you were going to say? Did you talk to anybody to have them remind you of certain details and events? Because it seems to me rather improbable for you to be able to testify about four years when you didn't work on the basis of your recollections or on the basis of what people said and in those particular years.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that you over there -- had you worked over there, you would have remembered things your entire life, because to bury 12 young men who were fighting for the Serbian people is a very difficult thing, and that is why I wanted to say what I know, because it would appear that the war boiled down to smuggling and that those young men had died for no reason whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was it who engaged in smuggling over there?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want to know who engaged in smuggling? You want to say that the war was actually smuggling? And you're very well aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly there were war profiteers, but do you want to say that the SDG engaged in smuggling?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. That's something that you're testifying about on the basis of your knowledge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean on the basis of my knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your knowledge and information that the institution, that particular institution, the SDG, because officially you were working in the SDG, were you not?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the Party of Serbian Unity. The Party of Serbian Unity headquarters and the SDG headquarters were in the same building. The difference was that when there were operations, Borislav Pejovic was the president of the party and the late commander was the commander of the SDG, and he was honorary president of the Serbian Unity Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But at any rate, he was the main personage in the Serbian Unity Party. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean Zeljko Raznjatovic.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Pelevic. Pelevic is a professor, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say. When I stopped working, he wasn't a professor at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But as you mention him in connection with the military activities, from the information I have, he dealt with the political aspects of the Party of Serbian Unity. He never engaged in any combat, military operations. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But during the Banja Luka operation, he did spend time, three or four days, in fact, in Banja Luka. And upon his return, when he came back, he told us that together with the late commander and also with General Talic, he took part -- or, rather, he said he defended Banja Luka together with them, as he put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that Banja Luka was on the territory of Republika Srpska and that, thank God, it is still in the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Prijedor itself is very close to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that. But I also know that Banja Luka in 1995 was on the brink of falling into enemy hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Is it clear to you, then, that the fact that they were defending Prijedor and Banja Luka, that that was a defensive operation, or rather, that they were defending those towns from the offensive that was being launched by the Croatian and Muslim forces in that part of the territory of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was no offensive. It was the defence of Prijedor and Banja Luka. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where do you see, then, in all that something that you don't consider to be in order and proper?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My testimony was not as to whether I considered something to be proper or improper. All I was doing was presenting some facts or my knowledge about them. So I haven't come here to testify, to say what is proper and improper or correct conduct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's okay. Yes. Now, you mentioned General Talic, and General Talic was the commander of the corps of the army of Republika Srpska precisely with its headquarters in Banja Luka. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they helped Talic's forces and they actually became part of Talic's forces, troops.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in that particular operation, don't you assume, then, that they had to be within the composition of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Guard took part in the area together, but it wasn't in the composition of the Army of Republika Srpska. The Guard, that is to say, the task of the Guard was, to all intents and purposes, to keep the positions from which the Army of Republika Srpska had fled, to maintain those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, they were there to defend the territory of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're not challenging that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on because we've been discussing different areas. You say that later on they made you the proposal of becoming a member of the special DB unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you filled out some forms, as far as I understood.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And from what I've read from your statement, you were not admitted because of your hatred towards me.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not because of hatred. I do not feel any hatred towards anyone. I was not taken on because I didn't share the political views of the then -- that is to say, the political leadership, and quite obviously the climate that prevailed was such in the DB that you had to agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you mentioned my name. You don't talk about the political leadership and the political climate and things of that sort, you say Slobodan Milosevic. So was there a question in the form which said: Do you like or dislike Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But it did ask what I thought about the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the Socialist Party?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, were you asked about any other party, what you thought about any other party?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they just asked you about the Socialist Party.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But yesterday you said that they didn't take you on because you mad had taken part in the 1991/1992 demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the second time they called me up and told me that I was undesirable politically because I had been a participant in the demonstrations in 1991 and 1992. What they do is they first invite you for an interview, you fill out a form, then a month or two goes by, they check out all the information you have entered into the form. That's the procedure. I'm speaking in general terms. And after that, I was told that I was a participant in the events of 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how did you get the idea of mentioning my name in your statement and linking me up to the fact that you were not admitted, not taken on?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The accused was the president of the Socialist Party of Serbia at the time, and I said after my work in the Serbian Volunteer Guard and the Party of Serbian Unity, but first of all my work in the SDG, I said I did not agree with the politics and policy of your party and your own policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as far as I am able to understand you now, from your explanations, you didn't mention me specifically at the time.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? In my testimony or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. In the interview that you had when you applied for the unit.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said at the time that I did not agree with the SPS policies and with your own policies and politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you think that that was the reason for which you were refused.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And not because of what you said yesterday, for taking part in the demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For both reasons; because of one and the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Tell me, how did you come to work for the Party of Serbian Unity the first time?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the first time.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first time they needed people to work for them at their headquarters. It was located in Savska Street, number 7 or number 9, close to or, rather, opposite the railway station in Belgrade. And an ad appeared, and I responded and I began working there, and I also became a member. I'll tell you that straight away. I also became a member of the party because they preferred having members work for them rather than non-members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you became a member of the Party of Serbian Unity exclusively in order to get a job there.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't share their political opinions, did you?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think about their political positions at all at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I assume that the work you were supposed to do there then was confidential in many respects, in view of the large number of contacts and your access to documents and so on and so forth, the documents that you're talking about, and there were many of those.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me correct you. When I was taken on board, all that existed was the Party of Serbian Unity at that time, because the Serbian Volunteer Guard at that point in time only had a camp open in Erdut. The headquarters were separate, so it didn't matter who worked there. And my job was to draw up the cards. So you didn't need anybody confidential, trustworthy for that, in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in one of the exhibits that were shown here - and I see that you have attached your entire diary - you have a stamp with the facsimile of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan's signature; is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have that stamp available to you?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1995 at the SDG headquarters I did have the use of that stamp. It was available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So the stamp with his signature was used to authorise and certify certain documents in his own name, so that they should be considered as having been signed by him.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, doesn't that mean that you were somebody of the greatest credentials and confidentiality if you were allowed to place the stamp with his signature on documents coming out of the party or the SDG?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only documents in the course of 1995 coming out from the SDG.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But if somebody gives you the use of a stamp which you can then use for any document whatsoever, I think we can assume that you were somebody who was very confidential and trusting, because if you wanted to abuse it, you could put it down on any document. And if you were entrusted with the stamp, that means that they had maximum confidence in you and that they thought you wouldn't misuse that highly placed trust. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if the witness wants to give any consideration to the degree to which she's giving more detail now about the use of the stamp and the issue that arose earlier. It's a matter for her, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The witness will have heard that. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, keep going.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can keep going. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Not to have to go back into private session again, and bearing in mind the facts that you presented and the ones that I quoted to you in private session, and the reasons and consequences that emanated from that, how is it then possible that a highly trusted individual as yourself, of that kind - how shall I put this? - how can they be qualified as -- or termed as a hostile element, if I can put it that way, in that group of people?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never a hostile element in the group. All I did was do my job seriously. It was just up to me to work, and I always took my job seriously, and that's what I did. I did my job properly. And I think that that's why they -- or rather, the commander had placed a great deal of trust in me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. As you insist that this be in private session, I should like to quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are not. We are in open session now. Now, are you going to go into private session in? Is this something that should be dealt with?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to ask the witness a more precise question, because you said that it shouldn't be mentioned in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness 129 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness 129, I hadn't realised that we were in private session still, so I asked a number of questions that would not require a private session. I had asked you about your notes which were given to me by the side opposite as some sort of a diary of yours. Now, will you please show on the ELMO, without any selection, ten or so pages from that diary. True enough, I can't see anything here. Will you please leaf through ten or so pages of that diary. Go on, please. Go on, please. Without any selection at all. I think that will be sufficient, so that we don't use up too much time, et cetera, et cetera. On various pages one can see that you need to wake up someone at a certain time or things like that. Do you call this a diary?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a diary of my daily duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what was shown on one page is your duty for that day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had two books, two notebooks. One was always in front of us at headquarters. It was a notebook for the duty person, who would write down everything. And then the next morning the page would be torn out from the previous day. And this other diary - and I have provided two notebooks - these refer to me personally, things that I myself needed to do. And I took note of those things in separate notebooks so as not to forget, because most things everyone in the staff would be doing. But as there were many events during the day, and if they couldn't do it, I had to note it down and do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is a kind of agenda and reminder for you as to what you needed to do during that day.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please turn another page or so. A meeting, et cetera ... lightbulbs, then a telephone. I have a page here which was apparently torn out of the agenda as an exhibit. They probably thought this to be something very important. It is tab 8. I don't know whether you can find that page in the diary. It ends with 1140. It's tab 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's given here as some sort of exhibit. This is the one that says "pistols."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 9, according to my records. I may be wrong. Tab 9, and if that could go on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. No, not that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Again, I can't understand what all this is about, to send something to someone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it here, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are we talking about? Start again. Start again, Mr. Milosevic. What is it you want on the -- what is the entry you want on the ELMO? What does it say? And then we can find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's given here as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Tell us what it says. And then we can discern whether it's an exhibit or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's tab 9.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my batch, it's 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is this what you want, Mr. Milosevic? "At 8.30, Erdut, pistols." Is that what you want?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO, please. Very well. Now, what do you want to know about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, since this has been exhibited, what does this prove, please?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see. On that day -- that day was St. Nikolas Day and it was being celebrated at the headquarters in Erdut. The commander had prepared pistols for the officers and men who had merits for the Serbian Volunteer Guard, and each of those pistols had an inscription on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So we're talking about gifts, are we?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, gifts as pistols.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Among us Serbs, it is quite frequent to give a pistol as a gift, especially to men.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But each of those pistols had a document attached containing a licence, a permit, from the military post in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The military post in Erdut could normally issue permits to members of the units belonging to it, because they were in Erdut and that was within the competence of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But allow me to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But those pistols just needed to be presented over there at a formal ceremony, upon which all of them returned with those pistols and wore them in Belgrade, with the permit issued by the military post in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it a problem that the authorities in Serbia recognised the documents of the authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just speaking of facts. I don't know whether that is a problem or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Nice asked you: Could Vukovar license plates be used in Belgrade? The license plates of all over the place were used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're going on to ask about license plate, it's another -- it's another topic. Now, have you finished with the diary or not? If so, can the usher remove it and we can go on with the rest of the evidence. Have you finished with the diary, or do you want to ask anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as we -- [no interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The interpretation --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does that telephone number mean that can be seen on that same page?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises, the microphone wasn't switched on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was asking you -- the interpreters couldn't hear me. What does this telephone mean on this same page?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can't remember?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My associates have checked. It's the telephone number in a restaurant at the Red Star stadium.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But is your building across the street from the Red Star stadium?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you called up somebody in the restaurant there at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please -- very well. Let us not dwell on that diary any more. I think we've established that it is not a diary but a simple reminder of your own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the diary go back to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice asked you whether the Serbian Volunteer Guard was also known as the Serbian National Guard, and you said no.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that Mauzer's guards in Bosnia called themselves the Serbian National Guard?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We called them the Panthers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You probably called them that later on, when their commander was killed whose name was Pantelic. But will you please now answer a few questions having to do with these intercepted telephone conversations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I would like to hear first, Mr. May, what is the source of those intercepts. Can we be told the source of those transcripts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to give the source at the moment, not least because the computer system is down and my ability to retrieve information of that kind is not immediately available to me. If there's no other impediment in providing information, I can do it after the break. Well, I -- I hope I can. Again, it may be dependent on the computer access.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then we'll leave that area -- that matter out and we'll move on to the transcripts of those intercepted conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before you were given the transcripts of these conversations, you were asked by the side opposite how Arkan arrived in Bijeljina. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.
