utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And your answer was that he came there upon the invitation of Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because he himself repeated that several times at headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, this transcript was rather later, some 20 days after these things in Bijeljina, when Biljana Plavsic called him up and spoke to this Rus.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rus. Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So according to my information, it was not just Biljana Plavsic but the local leadership and this same Mauzer who was the commander of the Serbian National Guard and who is also from Bijeljina. You know that.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the commander always spoke with pride of the fact that Biljana Plavsic had called him to fight there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. He spoke with pride of the fact that Biljana Plavsic had called him to fight there. Well, then was he sent there by the Serbian state security, or upon the invitation of Biljana Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: She invited him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it wasn't the state -- the Serbian state security that sent him there.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was only speaking about the Serbian state security during the period that I was employed at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. But you said in general terms in your statement, and I quote from your statement, on page 6 of your first statement: "Arkan did not fall from the sky. His units would never have been able to act in the way they did had they not been an integral part of the state security of Serbia."

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on the second page of your second statement, in paragraph 8, speaking about Arkan, you say: "Arkan was always on good terms with the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. DB. Even before the war, he was an agent working for the DB outside the borders of Yugoslavia." You said all that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what you're saying now is something else. What I quoted you as saying, you are saying related to the period after 1994. As for Bijeljina, you say that he told you with pride that he was invited by Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... try as possible to follow that question. Can you put it clearly what it is you want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All I want is to clear this up. According to your own knowledge - and I don't want you to say anything that is not part of your own knowledge - that he went to Bijeljina at the invitation of Biljana Plavsic and not by being sent there by anybody from the DB of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he had been invited by Biljana Plavsic herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, look at this transcript, please, of the conversation of the 23rd of April, 1992 that we listened to yesterday. And it says: "I still haven't reached home. A small section is blocked. But I wanted --" This is at the beginning of the second half of this transcript. Can you find it?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "A small section is blocked, but I just wanted, and would you ask him in principle if we were to call for him to come here, would that be possible?" So what -- do you understand her question?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. But all I was asked to do was to identify the persons and not to comment on their conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But does that agree with what your commander said to you about him going there upon the invitation of the leadership, or rather, one of the main members of the leadership of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this question relates to going there to some other location. Is that clear from this conversation?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, will you please look at it. It says, "I don't have the authority." And she says, "Yes, I understand that." And he says he will pass on the message immediately. "Please convey to him that once I am in my apartment, I will call him up." Yes. And then, "I won't ask him this." She says, "I won't ask him this, but I will only ask him whether he will bring those goods if he can." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that this will be in place of this question as to whether they could go there?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But yesterday Mr. Nice asked you what kind of goods were referred to. Isn't it clear from this conversation that this is an expression to be used instead of going there? Because she says, "I won't put the question in this form, but I will ask whether those goods can be brought."

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the Prosecutor Nice didn't put the question quite in that form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That will be a matter for us to decide. It's time that we adjourn. We'll adjourn now, as I said, for half an hour, and we'll come back then -- Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I raise a matter? It's to do with the scheduling of matters due to rearrangements today. It causes difficulty for us, for obvious reasons. Mr. Tapuskovic is in fact dealing with this witness. The other matters, the legal argument, was going to be dealt with by me. I doubt whether we're going to have time to deal with it today, realistically, but I had personal arrangements which it's impossible to break due to the particular date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It's unsatisfactory, completely unsatisfactory, impossible to get this work done. It's not your fault. Not your fault. We must finish this witness today. And Mr. Tapuskovic, I fear that your cross-examination will have to be necessarily very limited in order to do so. I will give a ruling so that parties may know what -- what the position is about those witnesses on whom we have ruled. Very well. We'll come back, finish this witness after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've got one session left. Mr. Tapuskovic, how long would you want with this witness, in the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I didn't hear your question. There was no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long would you want with the -- this witness, there being just this session left?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did my best to shorten it as far as possible during the break, so I think perhaps five or six minutes, maybe a few minutes more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice, one matter: We'll have to deal with these administrative matters first thing on Monday morning. It's absurd that we miss the opportunity so regularly because of circumstances quite beyond the control of the Court. But so the first session next Monday we will deal with the matters concerning the witnesses on which we must rule. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The microphone was not switched on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying we ought to go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we aren't in open session, we certainly should be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: My impression is we've been in open session for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at the second transcript of the conversation played yesterday, and that is tab 6. And talking there are Legija and Raznjatovic. I won't read out the whole of the transcript because I've already asked you about it, about what it refers to and who the speakers are, we've already established that, the stinkers and so on. But at the end of the page, he says that 7.200 refugees were stopped, and he speaks about Mladic, who was the commander of the military district at that time. I assume you know about all that.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I assume you knew that it was still the JNA which was withdrawing and being attacked. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then he goes on to say that he called Panic, the superior in Belgrade, and he says, "Panic said that they should be released," that is to say, that the people who had been stopped there - and he mentions 7.200 people - should be released, "That we are a humane people." That's what he said. And he's making fun of Panic a little bit for saying that, but without a doubt Panic is calling for the release of those people. He wants the people to be released and not to have them stopped. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's the transcript of that particular conversation.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I heard the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the only person, as we can see from the transcript, that they are communicating with in Belgrade, General Panic is insisting upon the release of those individuals; is that clear?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it also clear that Legija in this conversation speaks about an attack by the Green Berets which started shooting at the soldiers and convoy? And that is towards the end of the second page -- well, not really at the end, but what he says is this: "They should have released the soldiers when the convoy left the barracks. These Jukina men --" he's thinking about Juka Prazina, who committed the massacre of the soldiers leaving the barracks. Do you remember the event?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I saw it on television and read about it in the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And you remember events which did not take place while you were working there, and yet you know nothing about this event and the comments made in the Party of Serbian Unity, or the SDG, when he says that the main man for the Green Berets - and he's talking about Juka Prazina - he started shooting at them and they turned back. That's what it says, and so on. I'm sure you know about that event, do you?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not about the event, but I know about Juka Prazina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, this man, Juka Prazina, you say you know only from the papers, is that it?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he committed a massacre of a column of soldiers who were withdrawing from the barracks, and the JNA was withdrawing from the whole territory, in fact?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I also asked you who else came to the party headquarters, and in your statement it says that the late Zoran Djindjic would come by too. When was that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Djindjic was there in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the topic discussed? Why did he come at all? Do you happen to know? What was the purpose of his coming?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came in early autumn, which means September, when the Party of Serbian Unity was just operating at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know nothing more about that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you cease being a member of the Party of Serbian Unity when you left your job at the party?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean whether I stopped being a member?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said you became a member of the Party of Serbian Unity. Did you cease to be a member once you left your job in the party?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I kept my membership card.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you a member of the Party of Serbian Unity today?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm probably registered as a member, because anybody who left the party would still have a membership card and therefore be on their files.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're not a member of any other party, are you?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about your family members? Are they also members of the Party of Serbian Unity or perhaps members of some other party?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family members are not members of any political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As you spoke about volunteers yourself and said that the volunteers were led by Arkan or sent by Arkan to certain operations in Republika Srpska and the RSK, at that time did you know or perhaps comment or anything else, learn anything else about how many volunteers, for example, went from Serbian and Sandzak, in particular, the so-called men from Sandzak, Sandzaklija [phoen], went to fight on the side of Alija Izetbegovic? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about this phenomenon at all that people did?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I read about it in the papers, but I can't say anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as you say that the volunteers were mostly under the auspices of some DB, some state security, can you assume, then, that these volunteers were sent by the DB of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also speak about a forcible and -- forcible and irregular conduct on the part of the SDG members, the Guards, and you testified about that; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? What do you mean by "forceful behaviour," or "forcible"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said they looted, they perpetrated various unlawful acts, they mistreated people.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say they looted or mistreated people. All I said was that -- I just talked about the mistreatment of prisoners of war in Sanski Most during the operation in Banja Luka and also the prisoners who were killed in Velika Kladusa. And when I spoke about the looting and theft, if I happened to mention this by chance, I just meant the smuggling that went on. I didn't speak about any looting or thefts otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you did testify, at least I think you did, and I think you were a bit contradictory on this point, that a unit of the military police was formed within the Guards and that they were in charge of the members of the SDG, only them, for quite the opposite reasons, to prevent them from looting, mistreating civilians, and so on, theft and anything else. And then once the operation was completed, these were disbanded, this unit was disbanded. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, does that then mean that Zeljko Raznjatovic, or rather, the Serbian Volunteer Guard, had a code of conduct, rules which would not permit unlawful acts on the part of its members which could be perpetrated in the course of a military action? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, rules did exist, but the facts show that at times those rules were violated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But if a military police unit was set up to ensure, even by using force, the application of those rules, doesn't that mean that it was the position on the part of the command and Raznjatovic himself that any unlawful acts must not be allowed to take place?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the position and view taken. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you go on to talk about the prisoners themselves, and Mr. Nice asked you something in that regard. Your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. response was, "He said they didn't have any prisoners," that that's what he would say. And then you went on to explain that you understood that to mean that the prisoners were killed. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And at the same time, simultaneously, you are testifying to the fact that there was a man in charge of the exchange of prisoners of war whose name was Voja, I believe, and that he was working in the Party of Serbian Unity; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that same individual worked on the exchange of prisoners during 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Does that then mean that the prisoners were not killed? Doesn't it mean that? Or does it mean that the prisoners were killed, as you claimed a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prisoners were killed, according to my knowledge, during the Banja Luka operation and in Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you say to the best of your knowledge, where do you get the knowledge from, this information that the prisoners were killed?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talk about Velika Kladusa and Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's take Velika Kladusa first. What about that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wounded men, the volunteers who were wounded in Velika Kladusa, once they had been returned to Belgrade, as they were incapacitated and not capable of going back to Velika Kladusa, they would remain at the headquarters in Belgrade and they would talk during the day sometimes. They'd talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you at least from the papers learn about the formation of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia whose president was Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you know that Velika Kladusa is precisely the centre of that Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know from those times that the authorities of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia had control over that territory, the territory that was not held by the forces of Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... the witness. All she can say is what she heard, not what she knows from reading the papers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, she's talking about what she learnt and heard about, and I'm asking, Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you learn -- what you can talk about are these conversations. Did the men say that they were under the control of Fikret Abdic or anything of that sort? Did they say who they were under the control of or not, or did they simply say what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They just said -- they just talked about -- actually, they went there and were under the control of the units of Fikret Abdic; however, they went off together with the members of the Red Berets, and it was their task to train Fikret's men. But at the same time, they did take part in operations together with them, and the result of that was that we had two men killed and about ten -- between 10 and 15 others wounded. Now, after that, they would come back to headquarters to work there and they would talk about it, talk about how people behaved towards the prisoners. And I'm thinking about the prisoners on Alija's part, how Alija -- and some of those people are Zenica [phoen], Mali Rambo, Little Rambo, and Gvozdeni. Those were the men who were wounded in Velika Kladusa and later on worked at the headquarters of the Serbian Volunteer Guard in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, I just want to make one point clear: As in the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia the authorities were from the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, did they tell you who held these prisoners, who the prisoners were controlled by, whether by the authorities of Western Bosnia or your SDG?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those prisoners were held by the members of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia. However, the members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, as well as the Red Berets, also had access and were allowed entrance into the prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, according to what you know, were the prisoners mistreated by the authorities which had control of the prisons or were they mistreated by members of the SDG? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what they said, the prisoners of war were mistreated by the people who would be in prison at the time and the people who could have been in prison at the time could have been members of the SDG and members of the Red Berets and members of the regular army, that is to say, Fikret Abdic's men; all the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But do you know that the regular army of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia was in control of the prisons? I assume you know that.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were asked yesterday by Mr. Nice about the volunteers, and your answer was that they were -- had to fill out a form of some kind; is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You did your best to establish that no people with psychological problems or drug addicts, criminals, or anything of that sort applied; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as criminals are concerned, we weren't able to establish at first glance whether they were criminals or not because we didn't have access to any criminal files, to checking out whether they had any criminal files in the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was precisely my next question. That's what I wanted to ask you. As I made a note of this, your answer, exact answer to Mr. Nice's question, when asked whether they had any criminal record in the police, your answer was that you were not able to check that out because you didn't have the ability and possibility of doing so; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what kind of cooperation, then, are you talking about between the police and the Serbian Volunteer Guard in the sense of some sort of sponsorship, auspices, patronage or anything else, or command if you were not able to access files of that kind, you weren't on a position to find out whether somebody was a criminal or not?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We and the public security, or police, had absolutely no contact with them, but there were so many volunteers that it would be quite impossible for us to check each and every one of them out and to send requests of that sort out every day to the -- and send lists to the DB for them to have these people checked out and return the lists to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That means that you're changing your testimony now. So you did have the possibility of doing so, whereas you said you did not have the possibility of checking this out with the police, whether they had criminal records or not.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said we didn't have the possibility of doing so, that's what I was thinking of. There were just too many of them. We couldn't send out the information on a daily basis and have the information returned to us on a daily basis. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And you say that the state security of Serbia, whenever it lacked personnel to take control of a location, that they took members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard. That's what you said yesterday, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, which is the location that the DB of Serbia captured in Bosnia or anywhere else in the Republic of Serbian Krajina? Which location was captured by the state security of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I misspoke when I said "captured." What I meant was when they undertook certain operations, such as the one in Velika Kladusa, and they lacked personnel, then they called up the late commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you read the papers at the time and did you know about the establishment of normal relations between the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia with the centre in Velika Kladusa, the Republika Srpska, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the signing of trade agreements, and the possibilities that were ensured for the free passage of people throughout those territories and for the normal traffic of goods and persons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is something -- did you -- let me ask the witness. B-129, you're being asked about a whole lot of political matters. Did you in the course of your business or work know anything about any of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Move on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But didn't you read the papers, at least?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You could have seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is the question which I've said you can't ask. It's no point what somebody read in the papers. It's totally irrelevant. Now, move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't argue all the time. Just move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. You consider it irrelevant if the institutions of Western Bosnia, Serbia, and the Republika Srpska cooperated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want to continue with this cross-examination? If you do, you'll get on with it. Or otherwise, I shall take it that you've stopped and you prefer to argue about things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 6 of your first statement, or rather, page 2 of your second statement, in paragraph 8, you say that Arkan was an agent of the state security; is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that you heard this from somebody called Kale who worked with him.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that this had to do in those days to the state security of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And when I said that, I meant the state security of SFRY. I didn't mean that he worked as an agent for the state security of the FRY, as an agent, or for the state security of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, let us specify the period of time of which you say that he was linked to the state security of SFRY. That was during the period which Stane Dolanc, a Slovene, was still the Minister of the Interior, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad we've cleared that point up, at least. On the second page of your first statement, you say that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and Arkan cooperated very well in 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know that from some confidential source, I assume, because you weren't working there at the time.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that because the commander spoke about it. And even in the office he had a photograph of him with Badza - I mean, the late Stojicic - and later on, he removed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, since you said yesterday that he said something offensive about Badza, let me remind you that on the second page -- actually, the first page of your statement, but it bears the number "2," in the second paragraph, you say, "Smuggling was always a strain on their relationship." You're talking about the relationship between Arkan and the police. This is the paragraph in which you speak about Radovan Stojicic. And then you say, and I quote: "The police and the state security didn't approve of it. At least, that is how it appeared to me." But yesterday you said something to the effect that even they had been smuggling. Did I understand you correctly or not?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The state security did not approve smuggling to such an extent. They were aware that the Guard has to finance itself in some way, and part of the money came from them but not all of it. We had to buy food, clothing, and the rest. So that they tolerated it up to a degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that they tolerated smuggling at all? As you know, it is the duty of the police to prevent smuggling, and this was a constant issue that was addressed at political meetings, at government meetings, in police reports, and so on. And you say here that the police and the DB didn't approve of it. So are you saying that up to a point they approved, and beyond that, they didn't?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that there was a degree up to which they would tolerate it. For instance, for them it was normal for one truckload to get through but not two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That they would tolerate one truck and not two or three?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they made comments to that effect, or rather, the secretary with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which secretary?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frenki's secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally meet that secretary?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you knew her personally?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were on friendly terms with her?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say friendly. It was more of an acquaintance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in the examination-in-chief you were asked by Mr. Nice, when you spoke about Frenki and Jovica Stanisic, whether she ever told you whether they had commented on their relationship with me. Is that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said no.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right; no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I or any of my associates ever have any contact with you? Not with you personally but I mean the Volunteer Guard and so on.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about your personal associates, from your cabinet, from your office.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you say that they finance themselves among other ways by smuggling, and here there's a whole paragraph - I don't wish to read it so as not to waste time - the various donors of the Serb Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were donors too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then Mr. Nice interrupted you and said you'd needn't go on. You just read out Giovanni di Stefano and the Karic brothers. You said that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, on television, I hear the Karics denying that they ever sponsored any formation that waged war anywhere in the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not a matter of what the Karics said on television. No doubt they would say that. Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you're naming here attorney Tomo Fila, which is working for this institution here too. Was he Defence counsel for a member of the Serbian Volunteer Guard and was in contact with you on that basis, or are you saying that he financially assisted the Serbian Volunteer Guards?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was one of the sponsors, the donors for the Serbian Volunteer Guard. He may have -- not have provided money, but he could have assisted in other ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what other ways could he assist the Guard?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the help of his attorney's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which means he could act as Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But surely that's his job.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what's illegal there? What's wrong with that if an attorney is doing his own work? Regarding tab 4, you said, according to my notes -- but true, I only received that tab in English, not in Serbian. You probably compiled the list in Serbian, though, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you entered in the list members --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the list is in Serbian. It's on the right-hand side of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the basis of your recollection, I assume, you entered members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard and the Red Berets; is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, explain a few names for me, please. For instance, Abdic Fikret.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider him to have been a member of the Serb Volunteer Guard or the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you put him on the list as number 1. He certainly wasn't a member of the Guards or the Berets, was he?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Giovanni Di Stefano, whom you mentioned as a sponsor, and according to data available to me, he was a member of the Party of Serbian Unity.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And a general of the Serbian Volunteer Guard. Did he fight in any theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was given this rank as some sort of an honorary title because of his membership in the party and the reputation that he enjoyed in business circles.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And because of the money he contributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, probably because of the money too. But he didn't fight anywhere, did he?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you mention Ljuban Ecin. Was he a member of the Serbian Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a person who was with the guards in the area of Banja Luka. He was the leader of the Red Berets for Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't it say here that he was head of the state security of Republika Srpska in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore he's not a member of the Serbian Volunteer Guards or the Red Berets but, rather, the head of the state security of Republika Srpska. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you put the Karics in the list. Were the Karics members of the Serbian Volunteer Guards or the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That list was compiled to include all the persons that I mentioned who in any way whatsoever had any contact with us. They were not just members of the Serbian Volunteer Guards. I put on the list people who came into contact with the Serbian Unity Party and the Serbian Volunteer Guards in any way whatsoever. The Karic brothers even bought an ambulance for the Serbian Volunteer Guards in the summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is something else. Wait a moment. It is well known that they assisted medical institutions and probably purchased ambulances for many and made contributions to hospitals on a non-discriminatory basis. You are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I also know that they paid in money on the account for the Delijes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For the purchase of an ambulance?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They bought an ambulance separately and gave it as a gift, but they also invested money into the Delije cooperative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what is that cooperative?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Delije cooperative was one of the companies owned by the late Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that some sort of a business relationship?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if it's a company --

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the Delije cooperative didn't have any business with the Karics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How can you know that when you weren't in that cooperative?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Delije cooperative would bring us money and we would take money to them. The money from the bakery and from the cake shop would be carried to them and paid into their account. If they wanted to buy something for us, they would frequently say that they didn't have the money to do it. That firm was not working very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You put Mihajl Kertes the list who was director of the customs service for while. Was he a member of either of these?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not a member of Red Berets or the SDG. He would be the person to call when a truck would be detained at the border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you explained yesterday that that truck, according to the way in which you operated, just transited the territory of FRY from one border to another and went on to Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And then those same goods would come back to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what, then, has Kertes got to do with it if the sealed truck crosses the border at both ends and is not importing goods to Yugoslavia, what has he got to do with your smuggling when afterwards, in small vehicles, you transport those goods to Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because if the truck was stopped, it would never wait. Usually trucks had to wait for a long time. And once Milica [phoen] called up, and she was the secretary of Kertes, and she would be called by Arkan, the truck would be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he asked for some sort of intervention for the goods to be allowed to pass on to Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But for Eastern Slavonia, not Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But afterwards those goods ended up in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a matter of your smuggling and it has nothing to do with the customs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned Dusan Loncar. Was he a member of the Red Berets or of the Serbian Volunteer Guards?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have included Aleksandar Martinovic, who carried flour for Arkan's bakery, and he was a driver in the headquarters. Was he a fighter or a member of the Serbian Volunteer Guards, or was he working as a driver carrying flour for the bakery?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The flour is important because that flour was taken from the Red Cross and carried for Arkan's bakery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How could you get the flour from the Red Cross for the bakery when that is a commercial establishment? A bakery is a commercial establishment. How could you get flour from the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Serbian Volunteer Guard could, on the basis of something, I don't know what myself. Aleksandar Martinovic was a driver in the headquarters of the SDG, and he would go to the Red Cross and he would always say that he would have to wait until Frenki's men took what they needed from the Red Cross, after which he would take flour and cooking oil, which were essential for the bakery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Pause. Pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Matovic Tomo -- Mirko Tomo, as you say, a journalist who wrote about the SDG, was he a member of any military unit or was he a journalist who attended -- who followed the unit and informed the public, wrote in the papers about it?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a journalist, and he worked for the Party of Serbian Unity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he wasn't a fighter of any kind. Ask then you speak about Jugoslav Micic, Juga, who was a driver at the headquarters in Belgrade, and he died in Kladusa. He was one of the two killed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you allow for the fact that he might have perhaps been killed because as a driver transporting something was hit by a shell of some kind, or do you claim that he was involved in a military operation of some kind?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim and know that Juga died in action, in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're very sure about that. How come you know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you are not somebody who was there in combat with him so that you know that he was killed in action.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But when the body of a soldier arrives in Belgrade, questions are asked about how he was killed at the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know that it was precisely the leadership of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia that they were hired out to help as instructors, to help the army of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you, therefore, also know that the money which was sent for those purposes, you say through the SDG, was the money that the authorities of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia paid out for the jobs that they were supposed to do; that is to say, the training for the instructors and so on?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They received money from Fikret Abdic during the Velika Kladusa event. But it didn't stop there with training. The members of the guard were at the front. They fought for Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You also mention a female --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [redacted]. A matter, of course, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also mention a female here. Her name was Mirjana.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Mirjana but Marijana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Marijana. And you say that she killed a prisoner in Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was she a member of the Serb Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you had female members too in the SDG, did you?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was the only one, the only woman up at the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that she killed a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the wounded men talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you believe everything that people say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about Pelevic. Pelevic was a political figure. He is still the president of the Serbian Unity Party, and he's still a deputy today; right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was in the political realm of the Party of Serbian Unity. He wasn't a member of the SDG in a combat sense.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, it was as you put it, as you said, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Let me try and get through this as quickly as possible. I have very little time. Tell me, please, you spoke here at one point - and I'd like to ask Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you to remember, think back - that if something had to be transferred across Vrace, they would do it by night, something to that effect. And in fact, it was something being smuggled. Right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The smuggling didn't refer to the transfer across the Vrace. I was talking about some goods there, and I was referring to the period of the Banja Luka operation and after that. So this crossing point Vrace would be used. We would call up a certain number and our vehicle would be able to cross at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you are aware of the fact that our authorities, after the rejection of the Vance-Owen Plan at Republika Srpska in May 1993, introduced a blockade? Are you aware of that? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you also remember that the international monitors arrived to monitor and supervise the blockade?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that that monitoring applied to Vrace and all the border-crossing points?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how then were they able, with those international monitors in place, to transport all those goods and freight?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were just asked that whenever we had something for a unit which was located in Banja Luka, that all we had to do was to tell them at Vrace and that the goods would be delivered to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is that all you know about the whole business?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean the only thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that the international observers -- not observers, but controllers, were in place at all those crossing points?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's why we'd informed the DB when we were crossing. We didn't, for example, call in for the crossing at Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you also say that on two or three times a week you would talk to Frenki's secretary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And she would tell you that he would not be able to make a decision without approval from Jovica Stanisic; right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what she told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite clear here. How is a secretary able to tell another secretary and explain to another secretary what her boss can or cannot decide? What's that got to do with your line of business, your job? Who told you to say that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I follow you. Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, your claim is fairly absurd, and that's why I'm asking you. How is it possible, how come the secretary of a functionary in the state security goes into explanations as to what her boss can or cannot decide? Does that seem to you to be logical? I am putting it to you that you thought all that up or otherwise somebody told you to say that.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not something I thought up myself. It's her statement, her sentence, so I'm just conveying to you what she said. I didn't think it up myself nor did anybody suggest that I say it. If it is not logical, then it is up to her and not me. That's her affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that she explained to you how her boss worked and who he had to ask for permission, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I said that's a comment. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Something is not right. Let's get it right. The transcript should say, "That's a comment." Now, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be very grateful to you, Mr. May, if you would correct the transcript when they record erroneously what I myself am saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You could always -- you could do it yourself, Mr. Milosevic, if you're concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness 129, you said that Arkan would always go to see Frenki.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you never saw Frenki come and see Arkan.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He only came once, and it was early in the morning in the parking lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard you say that yesterday. So you saw him in a parking lot. You saw him coming in to his car or leaving his car.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was standing in our parking lot when I came to work in the morning. I asked the guard who the gentleman was, and he said that that was a person looking for the commander. Afterwards, I called the commander up, the commander came from home with the 05, and they left then, and the commander later on told me who the man was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were close ties with the DB. Did anyone from the -- was anyone from the SDG a member of the DB?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean during the war operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What I mean is throughout, throughout all the things and time you know about. Or let me be more specific. Did any one of them have an ID card affiliating him to the DB?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's fine. You also say that some sort of weaponry was transported. Mr. Nice asked you something about that. And your answer was, "Just pistols and uniforms." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He also asked you whether in Belgrade they could use vehicles with Vukovar license plates. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you also remember that people would drive around with number plates from all the former Yugoslav republics? You could see cars on the streets of Belgrade with different license plates, from Skopje, from Vukovar, from Zagreb, from Bijeljina, from Slovenia, and so on?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was nothing special in the use of Vukovar license plates. This was nothing out of the ordinary; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Fine. He also asked you -- Mr. Nice also asked you about money, the money that came in from the Velika Kladusa operation, or rather, where they were paid. He said -- he asked you where Abdic got his money from, and your answer was that you don't know. What do they have to do with the source of Abdic's money? Did you ever establish a link?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean links with Fikret Abdic's money or funds? How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The leadership of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, the authorities who engaged the instructors in the first place, and experts, professionals, from the SDG. They paid for the services rendered; right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was the money that reached you and which was used to pay out the people who did the job.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The money reached me -- only money for the wounded. They would be directly paid in the field, the fighters, the combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, in the field because they were there. And the wounded men who were in Belgrade, they would get their salaries from over there and you would distribute their salaries to them in Belgrade. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that money belonged to the authorities of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia. They were their funds. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Fine. Yesterday you commented on a photograph shown to you by the opposite side as being a photograph from Bijeljina, and you said that it wasn't Bijeljina but Brcko. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said that you recognised Srdjan Golubovic, nicknamed Max; right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that that man, Srdjan Golubovic, Max, had nothing to do with the killing or any responsibility for the killing of the person seen on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I said that too. That's what I stated, that to the best of my knowledge he went up to the woman when the woman was already dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the photograph was made when they arrived and tried to identify what had happened or to see whether it was a wounded person or somebody who had already died; that is to say, that the killing had nothing to do with the activities of the Serbian Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as that particular photograph was concerned, why they went up there, I can only guess. All I know is that the man Max said that he had a lot of problems because he approached that woman with a rifle in his hands, trying to turn her over, turn her body over. That's what Max told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he had problems because he was in the vicinity of a dead person generally. And as far as I understand it, you have no information or knowledge as to his accountability or that he was responsible or that any of the members of the SDG was responsible for the death of that particular individual. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You never saw Radovan Stojicic, Badza, did you?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you heard that he threw Arkan out of Erdut and that Arkan was angry because of that.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that he helped introduce law and order when he was invited to do so by the authorities of Srpska Krajina? In view of the fact that he wielded a great deal of authority, he was the only one that could have thrown them out of Erdut.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you yesterday mentioned Radovan Stojicic and his links to some kind of smuggling, as he was a very respected man and a patriot, do you have any knowledge whatsoever that he in fact did engage in smuggling of any kind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Just wait a moment. The accused is alleging that Stojicic was a respected man. Do you know if that's right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's your suggestion. All the evidence is that he was involved in the smuggling. Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. May. I understood the witness to say quite the opposite, that she has no information of him participating in any kind of smuggling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that right, Witness 129?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't allow me to complete what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, please go ahead, then.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the stories told by Arkan as to why he was angry, he was angry because of the camp and he was also angry because the two of them had, as he said, stopped the trading. And he was referring -- he meant the smuggling. Because according to him, Badza wanted to keep the bulk of it for himself, the bulk of the proceeds for himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. But in your statement you say that they quarrelled and that their relations became tense. And I'm quoting exactly what you said, "The police and the DB did not approve of it." They did not approve of the smuggling, in other words.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the period in 1995. That sentence refers to that period, the sentence you quoted. It refers to 1995. But I'm telling you now about my knowledge linked to Stojicic, Badza, and the comments or, rather, what the late commander said about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you have no other knowledge about any involvement of Radovan Stojicic in those dishonourable activities.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And when you say that their relations were not good, did all that happen in 1993?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, 1994, and until the end of my work for the SDG, they did not communicate, they were not on speaking terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. Their relations were not good, but you're claiming that it was under the sponsorship of the police that the Serbian Volunteer Guard went to various battlefronts.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the late Stojicic was in the public security service, and the Serbian Volunteer Guard had contact with Frenki, who was working in the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you then assume that the public security and the state security of the same Ministry of the Interior were engaged in two contradictory activities?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is -- you know that the Ministry of the Interior had two departments; public security and state security.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you now claiming that the public security and the state security services were doing -- working against one another, that is, they were in dispute with the public security while cooperating with the state security service? Can that be possible at all?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You saw Frenki having contact with Arkan. That's what you saw.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he was not having any contact with Stojicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you are now saying that the late Arkan confided in you, who was a student at the time and an administrative clerk doing a part-time job, he confided in you about his relationships with the highest level officials in the police; with whom he was on good terms and with whom he was on bad terms. Were you so intimate with him?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan was prone to commenting on his relationships in the office. When I say "comment on his relationships with others," I mean with people he was in contact with. So he would comment and recount these things. These were not confidential, non-confidential things. Whoever happened to be there could have heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So whoever was there, he explained to those people that Frenki had asked him that the Serbian Volunteer Guard should assist them.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, your previous question related to Stojicic. You were speaking about high-level officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Frenki, when he said that, he said that to me and maybe to three other people in the office. So he didn't comment on future activities with everyone, but he would comment on things from the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you're talking about this Operation Pauk, or Spider, and that Frenki called Arkan on the phone and to ask him for assistance and then Arkan told you why this other one had called him. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He just said that Frenki had called him and that I need to call a list of names that consisted of 40 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you were obviously a person of the greatest trust, tell me, under what terms did he agree on the engagement of his men in Velika Kladusa, since money was coming from there, salaries, and so on? So do you know on what terms he negotiated his involvement with the authorities of Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you do know that he made arrangements with them. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you in Velika Kladusa?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You even say that Arkan didn't go there either.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he wasn't there either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So neither you nor Arkan was in Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we weren't there. We didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. There's a contradiction which I'm unable to explain without your assistance. You said that the authorities in Velika Kladusa sent money via the DB, whereas on the other hand, that the fighters told you that they saw an Abdic follower giving money to Legija and him distributing it to members of the SDG.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there's no contradiction there. Men who were on the ground would receive money in such a way that Legija would go to see Fikret and he would get money from him and distribute it to the members; whereas, through the DB money would come which would be distributed to fighters who were wounded in Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So that was your explanation. So he went to the headquarters of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And those headquarters of Western Bosnia, were they in command of the operations in Velika Kladusa?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume so. I cannot claim that they were not. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us the names of the members of the Serbian Volunteer Guards who gave you that information so that we might call them here too? If necessary, we can go into private session for you to do that. Will you tell us the names of those people.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first person is Milorad Lukovic, Legija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you see Milorad Lukovic Legija for the last time?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When did I see him for the last time? In 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did he tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he came to the headquarters during the Velika Kladusa operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The position is this: Apparently in the building, so that everybody should know, there is to be a complete shutdown at 3.00. Everybody is going to be asked to leave the building. In order to give us sufficient time to do that, we will finish today at no later than 2.45, which means that, if possible, a few minutes before. Mr. Milosevic, will you bring your cross-examination to a close at or before half past. Mr. Tapuskovic, you will have five minutes. There will be no re-examination. I will give this ruling, which I have been meaning to give for several days and we will then adjourn. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I obviously will not have the time I should, but that is not the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You will have very nearly the same as the Prosecution. On one occasion - this will be, as far as I can see, the first one in the trial - you will have five minutes less than them. Yes. Let us go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Everything about this, as to whether Frenki went to Velika Kladusa or not and when, you know from his secretary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the secretary and from the wounded who were in Velika Kladusa, people who were in Kladusa and were wounded and then came to the headquarters of the SDG.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And who were the Tigers that you mentioned who told you that they went first to the centre at Tara, Mount Tara?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want their names?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nebojsa Djordjevic, Suca, Vlasdenovic [phoen], known as Gvozdeni, Slavica Stavanovac [phoen], known as Zenica [phoen], Zarko Aleksic [phoen], known as Marinac [phoen]. Those were some of the men from the first group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you know all that, tell me, how many men were trained at the centre on Mount Tara from among your members of the SDG?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were there very briefly, and that is what I said in my statement. They were there not longer than seven days. And I'm talking about the first group. I don't know about the second group. They were there for seven days. And after that, they were transferred to Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, what kind of training is that that lasts seven days? Do you have any idea about that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they were doing over there, so I don't know at all whether it was any kind of training. When they left, they spent a week at the camp in Tara. Now, whether that was training or waiting, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe it could have been a rest, a vacation.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it was a vacation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What else would they be doing on Mount Tara? Were they untrained for war operations, those men that you just mentioned? Were they men who needed training?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But do you have any idea what they were doing at Tara?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, why are you testifying about that, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on. That's a pointless comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your statement of the 9th and 10th of November, 2002, on page 4, third paragraph, you say that I and Jovica Stanisic were close. Who told you that? Was it Jovica Stanisic who told you that?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how do you make that inference?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the -- it is normal for the chief of the state security to be accountable to the president of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you are drawing a conclusion on the basis of the positions people held and not because you had any knowledge about our closeness.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was just a statement. I have no knowledge about you or about Mr. Stanisic. All I said was that, according to our law, it is normal and logical for the chief of the state security to be accountable to the president of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's very fine. I'm just -- I just wanted to know on what grounds you make that assertion. If you base it on the law, that's fine, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Only on the basis of the laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that Mihajlo Ulemek granted an interview to the Belgrade Journal Interview, after which Frenki called up Arkan and asked, "What is that fool of yours doing?" Were you listening in to that conversation?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. But the late commander told me furiously, "Call him because this Frenki has gone crazy and he granted an interview to the Journal interview," and he told me to send somebody to buy a copy of that journal so that he could see what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So he again gave you some explanations. But in your statement of the 8th and 9th of July, 2002, in the last paragraph on the last page, you say you were not familiar with the way looted goods were divided up.

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean on the ground, the looted goods on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm just asking you this because you said that there was no looting, which I believe. Therefore, is it true that the investigator asked you about how the looted goods were shared out?

utterances.speaker: B-129 [Resumed]
